title: The blindfolded man
hookLine: a man left blindfolded far from home, and why Hindus honor the one who unties it
carry: the guru unties the blindfold; you walk
tomorrow: the dying man and the fire ordeal

lines: SO WHY DON'T I FEEL IT?
A MAN WITH A CLOTH OVER HIS EYES.
cards: Honey and rivers, trees and seeds and salt. And still, maybe, Shvetaketu is thinking what anyone would think. Fine.
Being is everywhere, and I am that. So why don't I feel it? Why am I still lost?
His father doesn't scold him, and doesn't repeat the salt one more time. He tells him about a man led far from home with a cloth tied over his eyes.

teach.b: Suppose, Uddalaka says, someone leads a man away from his home in Gandhara with his eyes covered, and leaves him in a lonely, empty place.
The man turns and shouts, east, north, south: I was brought here blindfolded and left here blindfolded!
Then someone unties the cloth and says: Gandhara is that way. Go.
And the man, asking from village to village, informed and thinking for himself, gets all the way home. In the same way, Uddalaka says, a person who has a teacher knows. Look at who does what.
The stranger doesn't carry the man home. He takes off the blindfold and points. The man still has to walk, and ask, and use his own head.
And Gandhara was there the whole time; he just couldn't see which way to turn. Uddalaka adds that for such a person, the only delay is until he's released from the body; then he arrives.
And the refrain: you are that, Shvetaketu.
Here's the teaching, and it's why Hinduism honors the guru so highly. All week, Being was in the honey, the rivers, the seed, the salt, and in you. What's missing isn't the road; it's sight.
That's why many Hindus bow to a teacher, touch their feet, and give thanks on Guru Purnima: not because the teacher walks for you, but because they showed you which way home is.

how: Hindu traditions give the guru, the teacher, a place of honor, and many communities observe Guru Purnima each year to give thanks to their teachers.

o: one who has a teacher to point the way home
a wandering monk with no home or teacher
a teacher who carries students all the way

games.q: Priya asks: if i have to do the walking myself anyway, why do Hindus honor a guru so much? what does the blindfold story say?
o: the guru walks the whole road for you, so you owe them everything.
the guru unties the blindfold and points; you still walk, asking village by village.
you don't need one; the road finds you on its own.
games.why: the stranger only unties the cloth and points, and the man walks home. so, Uddalaka says, one who has a teacher knows.

practice: Think of someone who untied a blindfold for you, a teacher, a grandparent, a friend, an author, and see their face; remember what they said or did. They didn't walk the road for you; they pointed, and you walked.
Many Hindus bow to a teacher; if you'd like, bow your head to them in your mind, and let gratitude rise if it's there.

wordCard.voice: Acharyavan, one who has a teacher. Untied and pointed toward Gandhara, he asks his way village by village; so one who has a teacher knows.

orig.note: Sanskrit ācāryavān: one who has a teacher. ācāryavān puruṣo veda: a person with a teacher knows.

carryVoice: Your line: the guru unties the blindfold; you walk. Week three of year two, done.
